content: 1. Individuals at higher risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection include those from populations with elevated seroprevalence, such as mobile and migrant groups originating from regions with high or intermediate HBV endemicity, as well as certain indigenous populations. Additionally, individuals with a history of exposure or high-risk behaviors, such as people who inject drugs, incarcerated individuals, men who have sex with men, sex workers, people living with HIV, and close contacts (partners, family members, or children) of individuals with hepatitis B, are also at increased risk. 2. Clinical features that may suggest underlying chronic hepatitis B (CHB) include evidence of existing liver disease, such as cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), or unexplained liver abnormalities, including abnormal liver function tests or findings on liver ultrasound. 3. In all settings, it is recommended to perform hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) serological testing. For those who test HBsAg-negative and have not been previously vaccinated, hepatitis B vaccination should be offered. This is particularly important for children with parents or siblings diagnosed with HBV infection or with clinical suspicion of hepatitis, and testing can be conducted through communityor facility-based programs. 4. For diagnosing CHB in individuals older than 12 months, a serological assay (either rapid diagnostic test [RDT] or laboratory-based immunoassay) that meets minimum quality, safety, and performance standards is recommended to detect HBsAg. Laboratory-based immunoassays are preferred in settings with accessible laboratory testing, while RDTs are recommended in areas with limited laboratory access to improve linkage to care and treatment. 5. A single serological assay for HBsAg detection is recommended before further evaluation for HBV DNA levels and liver disease staging. Persistent HBsAg positivity for six months or more confirms CHB. 6. Infants exposed to HBV should be tested for HBsAg between 6 and 12 months of age to screen for evidence of infection. Testing within the first six months of life is problematic due to inconsistent detectability of HBsAg and HBV DNA in infected infants. 7. Acute HBV infection can be confirmed by the presence of HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc. Chronic HBV infection is diagnosed by the persistence of HBsAg for six months or longer. 8. Laboratory-based immunoassays, such as enzyme immunoassay, chemiluminescence immunoassay, and electrochemiluminescence assay, should meet minimum acceptance criteria, including WHO prequalification or stringent regulatory review. All in vitro diagnostics should be used according to manufacturers’ instructions and, where possible, at sites enrolled in external quality assessment schemes. 9. Predictive modeling of positive predictive values based on seroprevalence thresholds and assay diagnostic performance informs testing strategies. Repeat HBsAg testing after six months is a common approach to confirm CHB. 10. Antiviral therapy initiation is recommended for individuals with HBV DNA levels >2000 IU/mL and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels above the upper limit of normal (ULN), or in the presence of co-infections (e.g., HIV, HDV, HCV), family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis, immune suppression, comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease), or extrahepatic manifestations (e.g., glomerulonephritis, vasculitis). 11. Antiviral therapy options include tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or entecavir (ETV). For individuals with osteoporosis or impaired kidney function, or for children and adolescents, ETV or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) may be preferred. Combination therapies (e.g., TDF + lamivudine or TDF + emtricitabine) are alternatives if TDF monotherapy is unavailable. 12. Monitoring of CHB patients should include regular assessment of disease activity, progression, and detection of HCC. More frequent monitoring is required for those with advanced liver disease, during the first year of treatment, or if adherence is a concern. 13. Pregnant women with CHB should be reassessed postpartum, as ALT levels may normalize during pregnancy and are not reliable markers for long-term treatment decisions during this period. 14. Infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers should receive a timely (within 24 hours) birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine, followed by 2 or 3 additional doses, regardless of the mother’s HBsAg status. 15. Maternal antiviral prophylaxis with tenofovir is recommended for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA levels ≥200,000 IU/mL or HBeAg positivity. Prophylaxis should begin at least in the second trimester and continue until after delivery. 16. Updated guidelines aim to expand treatment eligibility, simplify diagnostic thresholds for significant fibrosis or cirrhosis, and promote equitable access to care. They emphasize a public health approach to scaling up HBV testing and treatment, ensuring access to high-quality services while addressing stigma and discrimination. 17. The guidelines target national hepatitis program managers, policymakers, healthcare providers, and laboratory managers, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, to develop and implement effective HBV testing and treatment strategies. 18. Simplified service delivery models are recommended to support a public health approach, ensuring equitable access to care and treatment for all individuals, including marginalized and high-risk populations.
